synopsis: ACARP C24028 was a University of Queensland haul-truck proximity-advisory interface project conducted in 2017, with follow-on work to 2019, using a modified haul-truck simulator [f3314, f15631]. The study found that richer schematic information reduced collision risk and braking force and shortened travel time, although a later experiment with fewer experienced truck drivers found smaller effects [f3316, f15632, f3317]. The booklet treats this simulator study as its main off-road evidence that operator-in-the-loop testing works [f15635]. Its public abstract reports no warning-to-brake reaction time, and an acceptable false alarm rate remains an open research question, leaving gaps for validation planning [f3318, f15633].

relations.note: Both identify the university project and its 2017–2019 timeline.
Both describe modified haul-truck simulator testing of proximity-advisory interface design.
Both report reduced collision risk, braking force, and travel time with richer schematic information.
Measured driver-performance improvements support the booklet's assessment of operator-in-the-loop testing.
The later experiment qualifies the reported benefits with smaller effects and different participant experience.
Later results show smaller effects rather than uniformly strong benefits.
The public abstract's missing reaction time limits what this operator-in-the-loop evidence supplies.
Evidence of testing benefits does not resolve acceptable false alarm rates.
